analysis.one_liner: Taxes opioid manufacturers a penny per milligram to fund state addiction prevention and treatment programs.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a hearing or a vote in any committee before Congress ended, despite bipartisan sponsorship.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would charge opioid manufacturers, producers, and importers an excise tax of one cent per milligram of the opioids they are licensed to produce. The money collected would be transferred to the Department of Health and Human Services and sent to states as grants for opioid research, prevention, and treatment — including new treatment facilities, recovery housing, and care for babies born dependent on opioids. It was introduced in October 2019 and referred to three House committees, but no committee ever acted on it before the Congress ended.
analysis.who_benefits: States and communities hit by the opioid epidemic would gain a dedicated funding stream for treatment facilities, recovery housing, counseling in underserved areas, care for infants with neonatal abstinence syndrome, and drug take-back programs. People with opioid addiction and their families would be the direct beneficiaries.

how_it_helps.text: Creates a permanent funding stream: every dollar collected from the opioid excise tax is transferred to HHS for state grants, with no need for yearly votes in Congress.

Grants can pay for new addiction treatment facilities, sober living homes, expanded residential treatment, recovery support services like jobs and housing, and care for babies born with neonatal abstinence syndrome.
Funds would also support recruiting and increasing reimbursement for mental health providers treating opioid abuse in underserved communities, and housing for children whose parents are in treatment.

analysis.who_pays: Opioid manufacturers, producers, and importers would pay one cent for every milligram of opioids in their federally set annual production quotas. Some portion of the tax could be passed along in drug prices, though the tax excludes drugs used for maintenance or detoxification treatment.

drawbacks.text: The tax is based on production quotas, not sales, so it falls on manufacturers whether or not the opioids reach patients, and the cost could be passed to prices of legitimate pain medications for patients who need them.
The excise tax by itself would not have addressed the drivers of the epidemic, such as overprescribing practices or the illegal drug supply; it is a funding mechanism, not a regulatory crackdown.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill paired a tax on the industry most associated with the epidemic with dedicated funding for treatment and recovery services, a design that keeps the money from being diverted to other uses. The main cost is a potentially higher price for legitimately produced opioid medications, since the tax is levied on production quotas rather than sales. On balance, the funding for treatment infrastructure would likely outweigh that cost, but the bill never advanced far enough for its design details to be examined or amended in committee.

outcome.mechanism: The bill sat in committee after being referred to three House committees and a subcommittee, and it died when the 116th Congress ended without any hearing, markup, or vote.

narrative.text: Rep. Max Rose introduced the bill on October 11, 2019, with five cosponsors.
It was referred to the Ways and Means Committee (which handles tax provisions) and also to Energy and Commerce and Budget, and four days later to the Energy and Commerce Health Subcommittee.
No further action appears in the record: no hearing, no markup, no floor vote, and the bill expired when the 116th Congress ended on January 3, 2021.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Opioid manufacturers avoided a one-cent-per-milligram tax on their production. Communities dealing with the opioid epidemic did not receive the dedicated treatment and recovery funding the bill would have provided.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Opioid manufacturers, who avoided the tax

for.name: Rep. Max Rose
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to tax opioid production and fund state prevention and treatment grants.

against.name: Rep. Richard Neal
against.role: Chair, House Ways and Means Committee
against.what_they_did: His committee, which holds jurisdiction over the tax provisions, never held a markup or moved the bill; it died there.

sides.party_line_note: The six cosponsors split 5 Democrats and 1 Republican, so sponsorship was bipartisan, though the bill's fate was decided by committee inaction rather than any recorded vote.

industries.note: The bill would tax them one cent per milligram of their federally set annual opioid production quotas, with proceeds going to addiction treatment. Killing the bill spared them the tax.
